competitors.title: Claude Managed Agents: The Complete Developer Guide (2026)
key_points: Three decoupled components: Session (append-only event log), Harness (stateless loop routing tool calls), Sandbox (isolated container for code execution)
Components can fail and restart independently — harness crash resumes from session log, sandbox kill doesn't lose session
Harnesses spin up in milliseconds (stateless), sandboxes provision lazily only on first tool call
60% reduction in p50 time-to-first-token, 90% reduction in p95 TTFT vs coupled designs
Session stores every event — Claude's context window is a selective view via getEvents(), enabling hours-long sessions without hitting limits
Pricing: $0.08/session-hour + standard token costs (Opus 4.6/Opus 4.7 $5/$25 per MTok, Sonnet 4.6 $3/$15 per MTok)
Step-by-step Python and TypeScript quickstart with ant CLI tool
Agent config: model + system prompt + tools + MCP servers; created once, referenced by ID across sessions
Environment: container template with pre-installed packages and networking rules
Built-in tools via agent_toolset_20260401: Bash, file read/write/edit/glob/grep, web search, web fetch

competitors.title: Claude Managed Agents: Complete Developer Guide (April 2026)
key_points: Teams building production agents from scratch spent 4-8 weeks on infrastructure before writing agent logic
Five core infra problems solved: sandboxing, durable session state, credential management, error recovery, scaling
Credential injection keeps secrets out of agent's context window via scoped per-session model
Disposable, isolated Linux containers for each session with secure sandboxed execution
Millisecond-level billing charging only for active runtime, idle time not billed
Clean separation: you own intelligence layer (system prompt, tools, model), Anthropic owns infrastructure (containers, state, security)
Versioned API layer separates intelligence from deployment concerns

competitors.title: Claude Agent SDK & Managed Agents: Anthropic's Q2 2026 Agent Infrastructure Play
key_points: Two distinct products: SDK (self-hosted programmatic harness) and Managed Agents (hosted infrastructure API, public beta April 8, 2026)
Three-agent harness pattern: Planner (structure/goals) → Generator (execution) → Evaluator (quality assessment)
Evaluator runs 5-15 critique-and-refine cycles, sometimes over 4 hours on complex tasks
Subagents are first-class with isolated context windows, returning only summaries to orchestrator
Compaction: automatic summarization handles single-agent long-session context overflow
SDK strongest at OS-level automation (native Bash, file I/O, subagent parallelism); weakest at multi-model flexibility
Neither offering complete: SDK leaves infrastructure to developer, Managed Agents doesn't cover data architecture/RAG pipelines
Enterprise early adopters: Notion, Rakuten, Sentry, Asana

competitors.title: Claude Managed Agents vs Claude Agent SDK (2026): Which Should You Choose?
key_points: Managed Agents: hosted REST API with Anthropic running the loop and per-session sandbox; app sends events and streams results
Agent SDK: library imported into your service, agent loop runs inside your own process and infrastructure
Both speak MCP and Claude models but very different operational contracts
SDK gives full control over tools, data residency, and cost; Managed Agents trades control for zero infrastructure
Custom tools in Managed Agents: Claude decides to call tool, but your app executes it and returns result via event stream

competitors.title: Claude Managed Agents vs. OpenAI Agents API — A Direct Comparison
key_points: Claude Managed Agents: $0.08/session-hr + tokens vs OpenAI Agents API: token-only (no session fee)
Managed Agents has native memory built-in (public beta); OpenAI requires manual vector DB setup
Managed Agents supports native multi-agent (lead + specialists); OpenAI uses Swarm/SDK patterns
Both create meaningful lock-in — migrating requires rearchitecting session management, tool integrations, and guardrails
Neither solution is cross-provider: both lock to their own provider's models
